items.prompt: What does the C in CAP stand for?
choices: Consistency: every node returns the same, most recent value
Capacity: every node can hold all the data
Coordination: a leader approves each request
items.explanation: C means every read sees the same latest value regardless of which node answers.

items.prompt: What does A (availability) promise?
choices: Every request that reaches a working node gets a non-error response
Every response is guaranteed to be the latest value
Requests are answered in under one second
items.explanation: Availability is about getting a response, not about the response being fresh or fast.

items.prompt: What does P (partition tolerance) mean?
choices: The data is split into partitions by key
The system has a backup datacenter
The system keeps working when messages between nodes are lost or delayed
items.explanation: A network partition is lost communication between nodes; P means surviving it.

items.prompt: Can a multi-datacenter system simply opt out of partitions?
choices: Yes, by using only two datacenters
Yes, by choosing the CA option
No, partitions are a fact of the environment
items.explanation: Links get cut and routers misbehave, so any system spanning a network must survive partitions.

items.prompt: When does CAP force a choice between C and A?
choices: Only while a partition is actually happening
All the time, even on a healthy network
items.explanation: With a healthy network a well-built system can offer both.

items.prompt: In the bank scenario, what exactly was broken?
choices: Only the ability of the two datacenters to talk to each other
items.explanation: Both sides were healthy; the lost communication alone created the dilemma.

items.prompt: Why is 'pick any two of C, A, P' slightly misleading?
choices: C and A can never coexist
P can be traded for speed
P is not really optional, so the real choice is C versus A during a partition
It is correct exactly as stated
items.explanation: Since partitions will happen, the meaningful choice is between C and A when one does.

items.prompt: When the network is healthy, what can a well-built system offer?
items.explanation: The trade-off applies during a partition, not at all times.

items.prompt: A team proposes a two-region database 'CA, because we will just not tolerate partitions'. What is wrong with this plan?
choices: Nothing; CA is a valid choice for any cluster
Partitions will happen anyway, and the design must still pick C or A when one occurs
CA is slower than CP but otherwise fine
It only fails if both regions crash at once
items.explanation: Opting out of P is not available to a system spanning a network. 'CA' just leaves the behavior during a partition undefined.
items.reference:
The three letters
🟦 C: every node returns the same, latest value
🟩 A: every request to a working node gets a real answer
🟥 P: keeps working when messages between nodes are lost
Why: partitions happen to every multi-node system, so P is a fact of the environment, not a feature you choose.
items.learnMore:
"Pick two" is a mnemonic, not the theorem

The real content is narrower: when a partition is actually happening, a cut-off node must choose between answering with unconfirmed data (A) or refusing to answer (C). With a healthy network you can have both.

Common mistake

Believing you can simply opt out of P by choosing "CA".
items.reflection: Think of two friends who normally share a calendar, then lose their phone signal. Who decides what is true while they cannot talk, and what does each lose by guessing or waiting?

items.prompt: A replica is reachable, but during a partition it answers every read with 'cannot confirm, try later'. Which letter has it given up?
choices: Consistency, because it returned old data
Partition tolerance, because it noticed the partition
Availability, because a reachable node returned an error
None, because refusing is always safe
items.explanation: A reachable working node that returns errors violates A. It has kept C by refusing to guess.

choices: No, that latency is a normal coordination cost; CAP's forced choice applies only during a partition
Yes, because W=N is required by CAP
No, because CAP does not apply to replicated systems
items.explanation: Coordination cost exists without a partition. CAP's sharp statement concerns what to do when messages are lost.

items.prompt: Datacenter B refuses the withdrawal during the partition. Which choice is that?
items.explanation: Refusing keeps the balance correct but gives no answer.

items.prompt: Datacenter B approves the withdrawal during the partition. Which choice is that?
items.explanation: Answering with unconfirmed data favors availability.

items.prompt: What is the risk of approving the withdrawal?
choices: The customer is angry about the delay
The link will never be restored
Both sides may pay out and the account goes negative
items.explanation: Approving without confirming risks double payout.

items.prompt: What is the cost of refusing the withdrawal?
choices: A legitimate customer is stuck at a working machine that does nothing
items.explanation: CP trades availability for correctness.

items.prompt: Why does B face this choice at all?
choices: It cannot know whether A already paid out money from the same account
B is not allowed to approve withdrawals
items.explanation: The missing information is exactly what the cut link would have supplied.

items.prompt: Is there an option that is both fast and correct during the outage?
choices: No, the missing information makes that impossible
items.explanation: Correct needs A's data; fast needs answering without it.

items.prompt: A 'like' counter shows a slightly stale count during a partition. Which choice does this reflect?
items.explanation: Nobody is harmed by a briefly stale like count, so serving is the better bet.

items.prompt: Which kind of data usually justifies refusing to answer during a partition?
choices: Data that is read very often
Data where a wrong answer costs more than no answer, like balances
items.explanation: The cost of being wrong versus waiting decides the choice.

items.prompt: A seat-booking system must never sell the same seat twice, and a short outage for some users is acceptable. Under a partition it should be...
choices: AP: accept bookings and reconcile later
CP: refuse bookings it cannot confirm
Neither, since seats are not replicated
items.explanation: Double-booking is worse than a temporary refusal, so consistency wins.
items.reference:
Two options at B
✅ Approve: customer served, balance may go negative (AP)
⛔ Refuse: balance stays correct, customer gets nothing (CP)
❌ No third option: fast AND correct needs info B cannot get
Why: B cannot ask A whether money already left, so any answer is a bet or a refusal.
items.learnMore:
The choice is about the business cost of being wrong

CP protects correctness at the cost of an unserved request. AP protects service at the cost of possibly wrong data and later reconciliation. Which hurts more depends on what the data is.

Common mistake

Treating CP as the "safe" default without pricing the cost of refusing legitimate users.

items.prompt: A news feed during a partition can show 30-second-old posts, but an empty page loses users. It should be...
choices: CP: show an error page until healed
items.explanation: Staleness is cheap here and an error is expensive.

choices: A CP choice with no extra work
An AP choice, with reconciliation work after the heal
items.explanation: Accepting writes while cut off favors availability and creates divergent copies to reconcile.

items.prompt: Which lean do ZooKeeper and etcd have by default?
items.explanation: They refuse writes on the minority side to keep one agreed history.

items.prompt: Which lean do Cassandra and DynamoDB have by default?
items.explanation: Every reachable replica keeps answering and conflicts resolve later.

items.prompt: What does a CP system's minority side do during a partition?
choices: Accepts all writes and merges later
Switches to read-only for everyone, including the majority
items.explanation: It refuses rather than risk disagreement.

items.prompt: What do AP systems do with conflicting writes?
choices: Prevent them with a global lock
Resolve them later, after the partition
items.explanation: AP accepts first and reconciles afterward.

items.prompt: Is a system's CP or AP lean a permanent label?
choices: No, many can be tuned per request
Yes, it is fixed in the code
Yes, it is fixed by the hardware
items.explanation: The table describes defaults; quorum settings can shift behavior.

items.prompt: Where does a system's lean actually show up?
choices: In how it behaves during a real partition
items.explanation: Healthy-network behavior looks similar; the lean matters when messages are lost.

items.prompt: Which description fits a Spanner-style system's partition behavior?
choices: Keeps every node writable and merges later
Sacrifices availability on a minority partition to keep one consistent history
items.explanation: It is a CP system.

items.prompt: An AP system after a partition heals must...
choices: Do nothing, since divergence is impossible
items.explanation: AP allows divergence, so convergence work follows.

items.prompt: A config store is used for leader election, where two leaders would corrupt data. Which lean fits and why?
choices: AP, because elections must always respond
CP, because disagreement about the leader is worse than a brief refusal
AP, because leaders do not need agreement
items.explanation: Split-brain leaders are the failure mode CP exists to prevent.
items.reference:
Default leans
🔒 CP: ZooKeeper, etcd, Spanner-style, CockroachDB
🌊 AP: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak (defaults)
🎚️ Many are tunable per request
Why: the label describes out-of-the-box behavior during a partition, not a permanent property.
items.learnMore:
Leans are defaults, not destinies

A system that leans AP can often be asked for stronger reads per request by raising quorum sizes. A CP system pays for strength by refusing the minority side.

Common mistake

Calling a database "an AP database" as if no configuration could change that.
items.reflection: Which tool in your own stack do you trust to agree on one answer, and which one do you trust to keep running with slightly different answers? Why is each the right fit?

Quorum sizes can be tuned per request so that W+R>N gives fresh reads
Strong reads require a different database
items.explanation: The lean is a default; W and R are the knobs.

items.prompt: What does strong (linearizable) consistency promise?
choices: Every read sees the most recent completed write, system-wide
Each client sees only its own writes
items.explanation: It is the strictest model and the most expensive.

items.prompt: What does eventual consistency promise?
choices: With no new writes, all replicas will converge
Writes are never lost to conflicts
items.explanation: There is no promise about when.

items.prompt: What does read-your-writes promise?
choices: A client always sees its own prior writes
items.explanation: It only tracks one client's session.

items.prompt: What does causal consistency promise?
choices: If B happened after A, everyone sees A before B
items.explanation: It orders related writes but not unrelated ones.

items.prompt: Which model is cheapest, with writes and reads never waiting on each other?
items.explanation: It requires the least coordination.

items.prompt: Which model suits a bank withdrawal best?
items.explanation: Eventual consistency could pay out the same money twice.

items.prompt: Which model suits a social media like counter?
items.explanation: Briefly different counts harm nobody.

items.prompt: Is 'consistent' a yes/no property?
choices: Yes, it is on or off
Yes, but only in SQL databases
It depends on the programming language
No, it is a spectrum of guarantees
items.explanation: Different models promise different amounts.

items.prompt: Alice replies to Bob's message. Carol sees Alice's reply but not Bob's original. Which guarantee would have prevented this?
items.explanation: The reply causally depends on the original, so causal consistency shows the original first.
items.reference:
The spectrum
🧱 Strong: every read sees the latest completed write
🔗 Causal: effects never appear before their causes
👤 Read-your-writes: you see your own writes
🕰️ Eventual: replicas converge, no promise when
Why: stronger guarantees cost more coordination, so choose the weakest one the product actually needs.
items.learnMore:
Consistency is a scale

Each model promises a different slice of what a reader may see. A bank balance needs the strict end; a like counter lives happily at the loose end.

Common mistake

Reaching for strong consistency everywhere and paying for coordination nobody asked for.
items.reflection: Pick an app screen you use daily. What is the weakest consistency promise it could get away with before a user would notice?

items.prompt: A user changes their avatar, refreshes, and still sees the old one, though friends later see the new one. Which guarantee is missing?
items.explanation: The user did not see their own write. Read-your-writes is the cheapest fix.

items.prompt: In W + R > N, what is N?
items.explanation: N is the replica count.

items.prompt: What is W?
choices: Replicas that must acknowledge a write
items.explanation: A write succeeds once W replicas ack.

items.prompt: What is R?
choices: Replicas that must ack a write
items.explanation: A read consults R replicas.

items.prompt: What does W + R > N guarantee?
choices: A read overlaps with the latest acknowledged write
items.explanation: The sets must share at least one replica.

items.prompt: N=3, W=2, R=2. Is overlap guaranteed?
choices: No, because W must equal N
Only if no replica is slow
items.explanation: 2 + 2 exceeds 3.

items.prompt: N=3, W=1, R=1. Is overlap guaranteed?
choices: No, because 2 is not greater than 3
items.explanation: A write on one replica and a read on a different one share nothing.

items.prompt: N=5, W=3, R=3. Is overlap guaranteed?
items.explanation: 6 exceeds 5.

items.prompt: Why does the shared replica make reads correct?
choices: It acknowledged the write, so it holds the latest value
items.explanation: The write could not have completed without it.

items.prompt: N=5, W=2, R=3. Is a read guaranteed to see the latest acknowledged write?
choices: No, because 2 + 3 = 5 is not greater than 5
Yes, because R is larger than W
Only if the write was recent
items.explanation: The formula needs strictly greater; a 2-set and a 3-set can fill all five replicas without overlapping.
items.reference:
The overlap rule
✍️ W replicas must ack a write
👀 R replicas are queried by a read
➕ W + R > N forces at least one shared replica
Why: a read set and a write set larger than N together cannot avoid sharing a replica, and that replica holds the latest write.
items.learnMore:
Pigeonhole, not magic

Choosing W of N and R of N replicas with W+R>N must share at least one. That shared replica acknowledged the write, so the read sees it.

Common mistake

Believing the formula limits how long replicas take to catch up; it only guarantees overlap for acknowledged writes.
items.reflection: Imagine two committees drawn from the same group of people. How big must they be to guarantee someone sits on both?

items.prompt: N=5, W=4, R=3. At minimum, how many replicas must a read share with the write?
items.explanation: W + R - N = 4 + 3 - 5 = 2 replicas are guaranteed shared.

items.prompt: What happens to write latency as W grows?
choices: It increases, since more replicas must ack
items.explanation: Waiting on more replicas takes longer.

items.prompt: Which setting leans AP: W=1,R=1 or majority/majority?
items.explanation: Both sides of a partition can keep serving.

items.prompt: With W=N and R=1, what is the cost?
choices: Any single unreachable replica blocks every write
items.explanation: Writes need every replica.

items.prompt: With majority/majority, what does the minority side of a partition do?
items.explanation: It cannot reach a quorum.

items.prompt: Can a system like Cassandra use different quorums for different requests?
items.explanation: W and R can be chosen per query.

items.prompt: Which setting gives fresh reads cheaply (N=3)?
items.explanation: Reads touch one replica, and writes already reached all.

items.prompt: Which operation gets cheaper if you lower R?
items.explanation: Reads query fewer replicas.

items.prompt: What do you give up when lowering R below the overlap threshold?
items.explanation: Reads may miss the latest write.

items.prompt: A product catalog is rarely written but must always be read fresh and fast. With N=3, which setting fits?
items.explanation: Writes are rare so paying for all replicas is fine; reads touch one replica and still overlap.
items.reference:
Quorum settings, N=3

items.prompt: What does last-write-wins keep when two writes conflict?
choices: The one with the higher timestamp
The one with the lower timestamp
items.explanation: Timestamps decide the winner.

items.prompt: Why does each stored value carry a timestamp?

items.explanation: Without one there is no principled way to pick.

items.prompt: A writes qty=2 at t=100, B writes qty=3 at t=101 concurrently. After LWW, what is the value?
items.explanation: The higher timestamp wins.

items.prompt: Is A's discarded write corrupted?
choices: No, it was valid but overwritten
items.explanation: Nothing was damaged; LWW just chose the other write.

items.prompt: What is LWW's real failure mode?
choices: It silently drops a real concurrent write
items.explanation: The loser vanishes with no signal.

items.prompt: What can vector clocks do that a bare timestamp cannot?
choices: Detect that two writes were concurrent
items.explanation: They record causal history, so concurrency is visible.

items.prompt: Which data suits LWW best?
items.explanation: Whichever is latest is exactly the right answer.

items.prompt: Does raising W to N remove the write race?
choices: It removes the need for timestamps
It prevents divergent accepted writes, at the cost of availability
items.explanation: Writes need every replica, so one side cannot accept alone.

items.prompt: Two users edit a document title offline, at t=100 and t=100.5, then sync. LWW keeps the second. What is the hidden cost?
choices: The first edit disappears with no conflict signal
items.explanation: LWW cannot tell the edits were concurrent, so one is silently lost.
items.reference:
Last-write-wins
🧑‍💻 A writes qty=2 at t=100
🧑‍💻 B writes qty=3 at t=101
🏆 Higher timestamp survives: qty=3
🗑️ A's write is silently dropped
Why: LWW picks a winner by timestamp alone, with no knowledge of which write the business wanted.
items.learnMore:
Lost does not mean corrupted

The losing write was real and valid; it is simply never returned. Detecting concurrency (vector clocks) or merging (CRDTs) can keep both.

Common mistake

Assuming LWW is harmless for any data type.

items.explanation: Only 3 replicas can reach each other.

🔒 W=3: nobody can write (CP)
⚖️ W=2: only the majority side writes
🌊 W=1: both sides write, conflicts later (AP)
Why: one parameter flips the behavior from refusing to serving, because quorum size decides who can still collect enough acks.
items.learnMore:

The same cluster and partition give different outcomes per write based on W. A majority quorum is CP-leaning because the minority refuses.

Thinking the CP/AP label belongs to the database rather than to each request.

items.prompt: What does clock skew break in LWW?
choices: It can make the wrong write look newer
items.explanation: Timestamps are only as good as the clocks that produced them.

items.prompt: What can replace wall-clock timestamps?
choices: Logical clocks such as Lamport or vector clocks
items.explanation: They track order without depending on synchronized time.

items.prompt: What is Spanner's TrueTime?
items.explanation: It exposes how wrong the clock may be.

items.prompt: What is a sloppy quorum?
choices: A quorum with too few replicas by design
A write 'succeeds' against temporary stand-in replicas during a partition
items.explanation: It trades the overlap guarantee for availability.

items.prompt: What does read repair do?
choices: Writes the winning value back to a stale replica it noticed
items.explanation: The cluster converges faster.

items.prompt: Does a strict quorum with W+R>N guarantee overlap?
items.explanation: Strict quorums use the real replicas.

items.prompt: Does a sloppy quorum keep the overlap guarantee?
choices: No, stand-in replicas may be read around
items.explanation: The acks came from replicas a read may not query.

items.prompt: Do quorums decide the right value among conflicting writes?
choices: No, they only decide which replicas to ask
items.explanation: Resolution is a separate rule.

items.prompt: A strict-quorum cluster with W+R>N uses LWW, and one replica's clock is 5 seconds fast. Which guarantee breaks?
choices: The overlap guarantee, not the conflict rule
The conflict-resolution rule, not the overlap guarantee
items.explanation: Reads still touch the latest write, but LWW may prefer a mis-stamped older one.
items.reference:
What quorums still miss
⏰ Clock skew: LWW can pick the wrong winner
🪑 Sloppy quorum: stand-ins break the overlap
🩹 Read repair: fixes stale replicas after a read
Why: quorums decide which replicas to ask, not which of the answers is correct.
items.learnMore:
Two separate guarantees

Overlap says a read touches a replica with the latest acknowledged write. Conflict resolution decides between values. Either can fail independently.

Common mistake

Assuming a correct W+R>N also fixes wrong winners or sloppy quorums.
